title: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak
hook: Sikhs and others mark Guru Nanak's birth with celebrations around the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, gur gaddi, and your line was the eternal guru. Today the counting reaches all the way back, to the first Guru's birth.

At dusk, the strings of small lights along a gurdwara roof blink on. Clay lamps line a wall. A procession moves through a city street, the Guru Granth Sahib carried on a decorated float, people sweeping the road clean in front of it, someone handing out sweets at the corner. It looks like a festival of light, and it is one: Guru Nanak's gurpurab, the celebration of his birth. When the count reached a round number, the lights went up in Punjab and far beyond it. Today: five hundred and fifty years of Nanak.
screen: `LIGHTS ON A GURDWARA ROOF.` → `SWEEPING THE ROAD AHEAD.` → `GURU NANAK'S GURPURAB.`

segments.voice: First, the celebration. A gurpurab is a Guru's day. For Guru Nanak's, Sikhs hold an akhand path, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, ending on the day itself. There are nagar kirtans in the streets, langar for anyone, and lights in the evening. Second, why light. Bhai Gurdas, in his first var, pictures Nanak's coming in a line people still quote: the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared, and light spread through the world. The lamps on the gurdwara roof are that line, made visible. Third, what scholars notice. The gurpurab is celebrated at the full moon of the month of Kartik, in autumn. Some early accounts of his life place his birth in a different month, in spring, and historians have discussed the difference. Sikh practice keeps the celebration where it is, and both conversations go on side by side. Fourth, the round number. A count like five hundred and fifty is just arithmetic. What makes it matter is what people do with it. When that count came, Sikhs and others marked it with kirtan, langar, lights and service, in villages and in cities across the world. The day wasn't about how long ago Nanak lived. It was about whether his light is still spreading.
screen: `A GURU'S DAY.` · `THE MIST CLEARED, LIGHT SPREAD.` · `KARTIK, OR SPRING?` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO WITH A NUMBER.` · then, large: `FIVE HUNDRED FIFTY YEARS.`

segments.voice: In the procession, people sweep the street before the Guru Granth Sahib passes. Bring to mind one person with a hard road just ahead, an exam, a hospital visit, a new job, a long goodbye, and with each breath out picture clearing one thing from it: a worry, a chore, a stone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do.
Gurpurab. A Guru's day: Guru Nanak's birth, marked with akhand path, nagar kirtan, langar and lights around the world. Today's word.
Your line: five hundred fifty years. The mist cleared, and the light spread. That's one thousand twenty-five days.

screen: `DAY 1025 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIKHS IN PUBLIC LIFE ABROAD.`

chat.says: Why are gurdwaras covered in lights for Guru Nanak's birthday?
options: Bhai Gurdas pictured his coming as mist clearing and light spreading. The lamps make it visible.
The lights mark the night the Guru Granth Sahib was first installed at Amritsar.
They're borrowed from Diwali, since the two festivals always fall on the same night.
chat.meaning: In his first var, Bhai Gurdas says the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread; the gurpurab lamps are that line made visible.
